title: Healthcare AI adoption is outpacing shared trust, with confidence varying by diagnostic task and perceived clinical friction
source_unit: Ipsos, The AI Trust Deficit in Healthcare, September 2026
geography: Healthcare professionals and patients; public summary does not disclose the full country frame or sample sizes

observations.period: September 2026; healthcare professional use of AI diagnostics

denominator.unit: Ipsos healthcare-professional survey; full sample and geography restricted to the gated report in the public summary

weekly_ai_diagnostic_use.unit: percent of surveyed healthcare professionals already using AI diagnostic tools weekly

adoption_route.value: AI-enabled diagnostic tools are becoming part of everyday healthcare

implementation_question.value: professional use does not by itself establish clinical validity, workflow safety, accountability, or patient acceptance

observations.method: Ipsos healthcare report summarizing survey evidence from healthcare professionals; the full report is gated and the public page does not disclose the complete sample, questionnaire, fieldwork dates, or weighting.
observations.uncertainty: The 41% figure cannot be generalized beyond the undisclosed survey frame, and weekly use does not measure tool quality, accuracy, clinical outcomes, or safe integration into care.
observations.subgroup: Healthcare professionals using or evaluating AI-powered diagnostic tools.
observations.counterinterpretation: Frequent use may reflect experimentation, institutional pressure, or administrative convenience rather than deep trust; clinicians can use tools while retaining substantial skepticism.

observations.period: September 2026; patient awareness of AI diagnostics

denominator.unit: Ipsos patient survey; full sample and geography restricted to the gated report in the public summary

patient_awareness.unit: percent of surveyed patients with at least some awareness of AI in diagnostics

awareness_trust_gap.value: awareness is widespread, but the public summary frames confidence as uneven and dependent on application

patient_stakes.value: diagnostic AI changes how patients evaluate explanation, responsibility, error, consent, and clinical judgment

observations.method: Ipsos patient survey summarized on the public report page; the complete design, sample, country coverage, and question wording are not publicly visible without registration.
observations.uncertainty: Awareness is not understanding, acceptance, willingness to use, or informed consent; the public figure does not establish patient outcomes or represent all patient populations.
observations.subgroup: Patients encountering AI-supported diagnosis, with potentially unequal health literacy, access, language, age, and prior technology experience.
observations.counterinterpretation: High awareness can support informed participation if clinicians explain systems well, but it can also increase anxiety or refusal when accountability and error pathways are unclear.

observations.period: September 2026; task-specific trust in AI-powered diagnostics

denominator.unit: Ipsos healthcare professionals and patient trust comparison; public summary reports relative application patterns rather than full percentages

higher_trust_tasks.unit: diagnostic applications with higher reported trust

lower_trust_tasks.unit: diagnostic or clinical applications with lower reported trust

friction_pattern.value: trust is higher where AI appears lower-friction or more bounded and lower where judgment, emotion, embodiment, or procedural risk is more salient

governance_need.value: AI adoption requires application-specific evidence, explanation, human oversight, and accountability rather than one generic trust score

observations.method: Ipsos synthesis comparing trust across AI diagnostic applications; exact task-level percentages are not visible in the public summary.
observations.uncertainty: Relative trust patterns do not establish comparative accuracy, clinical value, risk, or causal reasons for confidence; application categories may be interpreted differently by professionals and patients.
observations.subgroup: Clinicians and patients assessing AI across screening, blood-test analysis, mental-health assessment, and surgical guidance.
observations.counterinterpretation: Lower trust in high-stakes or relational applications may be appropriate caution, but it may also slow beneficial tools if safeguards and evidence are not communicated effectively.

related_sources.claim: Ipsos Global Trustworthiness Index provides complementary profession and AI-chatbot trust context.
WEF emerging-technology foresight provides complementary governance, access, and trust context for AI-enabled health technologies.
WHO ethics and governance work provides complementary health-AI safety, accountability, and equity context.

boundary: This record adds a health-AI adoption route linking clinician use, patient awareness, task-specific trust, clinical friction, explanation, oversight, and accountability. The public Ipsos summary provides only selected findings from a gated report, so this is not a full representative dataset, diagnostic accuracy evaluation, clinical outcomes study, or proof of safe adoption.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: The official Ipsos report page and gated download landing page were reviewed for the public sample-free summary, weekly professional use, patient awareness, application-specific trust pattern, and access limitations; the full report was not publicly available without registration.
